items.q: (A) No sooner the referee had blown the final whistle (B) than thousands of supporters (C) began streaming towards the exits, (D) convinced their team's season was over.
options: No sooner the referee had blown the final whistle
convinced their team's season was over
items.correction: No sooner had the referee blown the final whistle
items.explanation: When a negative adverbial such as No sooner opens the sentence, subject and auxiliary invert: No sooner had the referee blown.

items.q: The head teacher demanded (A) that every pupil (B) hands in the permission slip (C) by Friday, (D) failing which the museum trip would be cancelled.
options: failing which the museum trip would be cancelled
items.correction: hand in the permission slip
items.explanation: After verbs like demand, insist, suggest the that-clause takes the subjunctive (base form): that every pupil hand in, with no -s.

items.q: (A) Had the expedition (B) packed lighter equipment, (C) they will have reached the summit by now (D) instead of camping halfway up the glacier.
options: they will have reached the summit by now
instead of camping halfway up the glacier
items.correction: they would have reached the summit by now
items.explanation: Had the expedition packed is an inverted third conditional (an unreal past), so the result clause needs would have + past participle, not will have.

items.q: Although the recipe (A) looked deceptively simple, the sauce (B) split twice before Minh (C) finally realised he had been (D) doing a crucial mistake.
items.correction: making a crucial mistake
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with mistake is make, never do: you make a mistake.

items.q: (A) Having read the essay twice, (B) several gaps in the argument (C) became obvious, (D) not least its reliance on a single unnamed source.
options: not least its reliance on a single unnamed source
items.correction: After the examiner had read the essay twice
items.explanation: A participle clause must share its subject with the main clause; several gaps cannot read an essay, so this is a dangling modifier and needs a stated subject.

items.q: (A) If only the weather forecasters (B) would have warned us earlier, (C) we could have moved the wedding (D) indoors before the storm broke.
options: we could have moved the wedding
items.correction: had warned us earlier
items.explanation: If only / wish about a past regret takes the past perfect (had warned); would have belongs only in the result clause.

items.q: (A) It was not until the final lap (B) that the Kenyan runner (C) did she pull away from the pack, (D) leaving the favourites trailing by several metres.
options: It was not until the final lap
did she pull away from the pack
leaving the favourites trailing by several metres
items.correction: pulled away from the pack
items.explanation: In the cleft It was not until … that … the that-clause keeps normal word order; inversion (did she pull) is used only when Not until itself opens the sentence.

items.q: (A) Despite the government's promises, (B) there has been (C) remarkably little investment in rural clinics and (D) far fewer equipment than the doctors were promised.
options: remarkably little investment in rural clinics and
far fewer equipment than the doctors were promised
items.correction: far less equipment than the doctors were promised
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes less; fewer is reserved for plural countable nouns.

items.q: (A) So a violent storm swept across the island (B) that the ferry service was suspended (C) for three days, (D) stranding hundreds of tourists in the harbour.
options: So a violent storm swept across the island
that the ferry service was suspended
stranding hundreds of tourists in the harbour
items.correction: Such a violent storm swept across the island
items.explanation: Before a/an + adjective + noun the intensifier is such (such a violent storm … that); so goes directly before an adjective or adverb.

items.q: Hardly (A) had the orchestra tuned up (B) than the fire alarm went off, (C) forcing the entire audience (D) out onto the rainy pavement.
options: than the fire alarm went off
items.correction: when the fire alarm went off
items.explanation: Hardly/Scarcely … when is the fixed pair; than pairs only with No sooner.

items.q: (A) The council pressed ahead with the bypass (B) at enormous cost, (C) despite the residents had voted against it (D) in two separate consultations.
options: The council pressed ahead with the bypass
despite the residents had voted against it
items.correction: although the residents had voted against it
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause with a finite verb; a subject + verb needs the conjunction although (or despite the residents having voted).

items.q: (A) A good field biologist must be patient enough (B) to wait for hours, (C) observant enough to notice tiny changes, and (D) sufficiently tough for tolerating harsh weather.
options: A good field biologist must be patient enough
observant enough to notice tiny changes, and
sufficiently tough for tolerating harsh weather
items.correction: tough enough to tolerate harsh weather
items.explanation: Adjective + enough is followed by a to-infinitive, and the third item must be parallel to the first two: tough enough to tolerate.

items.q: (A) Under no circumstances the lab doors should be propped open (B) while the centrifuge is running, (C) however stuffy (D) the room becomes.
options: Under no circumstances the lab doors should be propped open
items.correction: Under no circumstances should the lab doors be propped open
items.explanation: A fronted negative phrase such as Under no circumstances forces inversion of the auxiliary and subject: should the lab doors be.

items.q: (A) The curator wishes (B) the museum bought the painting (C) when it came up for auction in 1998, (D) rather than losing it to a private collector.
options: when it came up for auction in 1998
rather than losing it to a private collector
items.correction: the museum had bought the painting
items.explanation: A wish about something that did not happen in the past (in 1998) takes the past perfect: wishes the museum had bought.

items.q: (A) If Lan were (B) a more confident speaker, (C) she would accept the invitation (D) to speak at last month's graduation ceremony.
options: to speak at last month's graduation ceremony
items.correction: she would have accepted the invitation
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a present, permanent condition (were) with a past result (last month), so the result needs would have accepted.

items.q: (A) Scarcely a week goes by (B) without some new gadget (C) being hailed as revolutionary, (D) usually at the expense to last year's model.
options: usually at the expense to last year's model
items.correction: usually at the expense of last year's model
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is at the expense of something; no other preposition fits.

items.q: (A) The rapid expand of the city's suburbs (B) has placed enormous strain (C) on a rail network (D) designed for a population half its current size.
options: The rapid expand of the city's suburbs
designed for a population half its current size
items.correction: The rapid expansion of the city's suburbs
items.explanation: After the + adjective the sentence needs a noun as its subject, so the verb expand must be nominalised to expansion.

items.q: (A) The coach reminded the players (B) that whomever scored first (C) would be excused (D) from the next morning's drills.
items.correction: that whoever scored first
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of scored inside its own clause, so the subject form whoever is required; whomever is only an object form.

items.q: (A) Attached to the application form (B) that you submitted (C) is two references and a transcript, (D) none of which has been stamped.
options: is two references and a transcript
none of which has been stamped
items.correction: are two references and a transcript
items.explanation: In an inverted sentence the verb still agrees with the subject that follows it; two references and a transcript is plural, so are.

items.q: (A) The more thoroughly (B) the students revised, (C) the less anxious they felt, (D) although the exam was far harder as expected.
options: although the exam was far harder as expected
items.correction: although the exam was far harder than expected
items.explanation: A comparative (harder) is completed by than, not as; as … as is used only for equality.

items.q: (A) The retiring headmistress did a heartfelt speech (B) at the assembly, (C) in which she urged pupils (D) to take nothing for granted.
options: The retiring headmistress did a heartfelt speech
items.correction: The retiring headmistress gave a heartfelt speech
items.explanation: The collocation is give (or make) a speech; do a speech is not standard English.

items.q: (A) Last summer the guide warned us (B) that the tide will turn within the hour (C) and that anyone still on the causeway (D) would be cut off.
options: Last summer the guide warned us
that the tide will turn within the hour
and that anyone still on the causeway
items.correction: that the tide would turn within the hour
items.explanation: The reporting verb is in the past (warned … last summer), so will shifts back to would, matching would be cut off in the second clause.

items.q: (A) The bakery on the corner, (B) whose owner trained in Lyon, (C) sells the croissants which everyone in the neighbourhood queues for them (D) on Sunday mornings.
options: sells the croissants which everyone in the neighbourhood queues for them
items.correction: sells the croissants which everyone in the neighbourhood queues for
items.explanation: The relative pronoun which already stands for the croissants as the object of for, so the extra pronoun them must be removed.

items.q: (A) Having veered north overnight, (B) the typhoon spared the coastal villages, (C) leaving behind (D) nothing worse than a few roads submerging under water.
options: the typhoon spared the coastal villages
nothing worse than a few roads submerging under water
items.correction: nothing worse than a few roads submerged under water
items.explanation: The roads do not submerge anything; they are submerged, so the reduced relative clause needs the past participle submerged (passive), not the -ing form.

items.q: (A) A great deal of the applicants (B) had never set foot in a laboratory, (C) which explains why the induction session (D) ran an hour over schedule.
options: A great deal of the applicants
had never set foot in a laboratory
which explains why the induction session
items.correction: A great many of the applicants
items.explanation: A great deal of is used only with uncountable nouns; with a plural countable noun like applicants use a great many of or many of.

items.q: (A) The lecture on Renaissance art (B) was delivered by the Professor Hale, (C) whose books on Florence (D) have been translated into a dozen languages.
options: was delivered by the Professor Hale
have been translated into a dozen languages
items.correction: was delivered by Professor Hale
items.explanation: A title used with a person's name (Professor Hale, Doctor Lam) is a proper noun and takes no article.

items.q: (A) Scarcely had the snow stopped falling (B) when the children (C) have dragged their sledges (D) to the top of the hill.
options: Scarcely had the snow stopped falling
to the top of the hill
items.correction: dragged their sledges
items.explanation: In Scarcely had … when … the first action is past perfect and the second, which follows it, is past simple: when the children dragged.

items.q: (A) Were it not for (B) her grandmother's encouragement, (C) Thu would never have taken up the violin (D) and would not have been performing at tonight's concert.
options: Thu would never have taken up the violin
and would not have been performing at tonight's concert
items.correction: and would not be performing at tonight's concert
items.explanation: Tonight's concert is a present/future result, so this half of the mixed conditional needs would be performing; would have been is for past results only.

items.q: (A) Both the lyrics as well as the melody (B) were written in a single afternoon (C) by a songwriter who had never previously (D) set foot in a studio.
options: Both the lyrics as well as the melody
were written in a single afternoon
by a songwriter who had never previously
items.correction: Both the lyrics and the melody
items.explanation: Both is a correlative conjunction that pairs only with and; it cannot be completed by as well as.

items.q: (A) The physics teacher, (B) along with two of her colleagues, are attending (C) a conference on renewable energy (D) in Da Nang next month.
options: along with two of her colleagues, are attending
items.correction: along with two of her colleagues, is attending
items.explanation: A phrase introduced by along with, as well as or together with does not change the number of the subject; the physics teacher is singular, so is attending.

items.q: (A) It was the goalkeeper's mistake, (B) not the striker's brilliance, (C) what cost the team the final (D) in the dying seconds.
options: what cost the team the final
items.correction: that cost the team the final
items.explanation: An it-cleft (It was X …) is completed by that (or which/who), never by what, which contains its own antecedent.

items.q: (A) After the merger fell through, (B) the two founders (C) grew apart and (D) eventually parted company at bitter terms.
options: eventually parted company at bitter terms
items.correction: eventually parted company on bitter terms
items.explanation: The idiom describing the state of a relationship is on good/bad/bitter terms; at is not used with terms in this sense.

items.q: (A) The astronomer's most controversially claim (B) was that the faint signal (C) could not be explained (D) by any known natural process.
items.correction: The astronomer's most controversial claim
items.explanation: A word that modifies the noun claim must be an adjective (controversial); the adverb controversially can only modify a verb or adjective.

items.q: (A) By the time the rescue helicopter reached the ridge, (B) the climbers were sheltering in a crevice for six hours (C) and two of them (D) were showing signs of hypothermia.
options: By the time the rescue helicopter reached the ridge
the climbers were sheltering in a crevice for six hours
items.correction: the climbers had been sheltering in a crevice for six hours
items.explanation: By the time + past simple marks a point before which an action had been continuing (for six hours), so the past perfect continuous had been sheltering is needed.

items.q: (A) Having grown up by the sea, (B) Bích found (C) the life in a landlocked city (D) oddly suffocating at first.
options: Having grown up by the sea
the life in a landlocked city
items.correction: life in a landlocked city
items.explanation: Life used in its general, abstract sense takes no article: life in a landlocked city, just like life at sea.

items.q: (A) Even after the second reading, (B) the poem made (C) hardly any sense to the class, (D) and the teacher's notes did not help neither.
options: hardly any sense to the class
and the teacher's notes did not help neither
items.correction: and the teacher's notes did not help either
items.explanation: After a negative verb (did not help) the additive word is either; neither already carries a negative and would create a double negative.

items.q: (A) I wish I can remember (B) where I left the key (C) to the shed, (D) because the lawnmower is locked inside.
options: because the lawnmower is locked inside
items.correction: I wish I could remember
items.explanation: A wish about the present is unreal and takes a past form: wish I could remember, not can.

items.q: (A) The village where my grandfather was born, (B) which name no longer appears on modern maps, (C) was flooded (D) when the reservoir was built in the 1960s.
options: The village where my grandfather was born
which name no longer appears on modern maps
when the reservoir was built in the 1960s
items.correction: whose name no longer appears on modern maps
items.explanation: Possession inside a relative clause (the village's name) is expressed with whose; which cannot act as a possessive determiner.

items.q: (A) Of the three routes up the mountain, (B) the eastern ridge is (C) by far the more demanding, (D) though it rewards climbers with the finest views.
options: Of the three routes up the mountain
though it rewards climbers with the finest views
items.correction: by far the most demanding
items.explanation: Comparing one item against three routes calls for the superlative the most demanding; the more is only for a choice between two.

items.q: (A) With the roof leaking (B) in three places, (C) it is high time (D) the school board approves the repairs it promised.
options: the school board approves the repairs it promised
items.correction: the school board approved the repairs it promised
items.explanation: It is (high) time is followed by a past simple verb with present meaning (an unreal past): high time the board approved.
